title: Google Axes Gemini’s “Gems,” Shifts to New “Skills” Feature – TechCrunch Report
body:
Google announced that it will retire the “Gems” feature of its Gemini AI platform, a move that signals a strategic shift toward a new generation of “skills”‑based agents. The decision comes as a wave of all‑in‑one AI assistants—such as Meta’s Muse and Instinct—gain traction, prompting the search‑engine giant to rethink how developers and end‑users create and deploy task‑specific AI helpers. By sunseting Gems, Google aims to consolidate its AI offerings under a more flexible, extensible framework that can keep pace with rapidly evolving user expectations and competitive pressures.

Gems, introduced earlier this year, allowed users to assemble custom AI assistants by chaining together pre‑built prompts and tool integrations. The feature was marketed as a low‑code solution for businesses and power users who wanted to tailor Gemini’s conversational abilities to niche workflows—ranging from scheduling meetings to summarizing legal documents. While the concept attracted early interest, adoption lagged behind the broader industry trend toward “skills” ecosystems, where modular capabilities can be added, removed, or updated without re‑engineering an entire agent.

The shift to skills aligns Google’s roadmap with the architecture it has been championing for its cloud‑based AI services. Skills are essentially plug‑in modules that end‑users can invoke on demand, each encapsulating a discrete function such as image generation, code debugging, or real‑time translation. Unlike Gems, which required users to define a relatively static sequence of actions, skills can be dynamically selected by Gemini based on context, delivering a more fluid and adaptive conversational experience. Google’s engineering teams say the new framework also simplifies compliance and security management, as each skill can be audited and sandboxed independently.

Industry analysts view the move as both a defensive and an opportunistic maneuver. On the defensive side, Google faces mounting competition from rivals that have already embraced skill‑centric models. Meta’s Muse, for example, offers a marketplace where developers publish and monetize micro‑services that the assistant can call instantly. Similarly, Instinct’s open‑source skill library has fostered a vibrant community that accelerates innovation. By deprecating Gems, Google eliminates a product that could be perceived as a half‑measure, and redirects resources toward a more future‑proof architecture that can integrate third‑party contributions at scale.

From an opportunistic perspective, the skills approach opens new revenue streams. Google can charge developers for premium skill hosting, usage‑based billing, or advanced analytics tied to skill performance. Moreover, the modular design encourages cross‑product synergy: skills built for Gemini could be repurposed for Google Workspace, Android, or even the company’s upcoming hardware devices. This interoperability could reinforce Google’s ecosystem lock‑in, offering a compelling alternative to the siloed assistants offered by competitors.

The transition will not be instantaneous. Google has given existing Gems users a six‑month window to migrate their configurations to the new skills platform, providing migration tools and documentation to ease the process. Early adopters who have built complex workflows are advised to audit their dependencies and prioritize the most critical functionalities for conversion. Google’s product lead emphasized that the retirement of Gems does not mean the end of customization; rather, it represents an evolution toward a more robust, scalable, and developer‑friendly paradigm.

Looking ahead, the success of Google’s skills strategy will hinge on the breadth and quality of the modules that populate its marketplace, as well as the company’s ability to attract third‑party developers. If Google can cultivate a thriving ecosystem that rivals the momentum behind Muse and Instinct, it may reassert its leadership in conversational AI and set new standards for how intelligent assistants are built and consumed. The coming months will reveal whether the skills‑first vision can translate into tangible user benefits and sustainable growth for the tech titan.
